question: The European Cloud Certification Scheme aims to harmonise European requirements in terms of personal data security. The EU Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) initially proposed three levels of risk for data storage: ‘low’, ‘substantial’ and ‘high’. The ‘high’ risk level applied to the most sensitive data (defence, health, etc.) and meant that the data had to be stored in Europe.
The ‘high’ risk level also required non-European companies (Amazon, Apple, Google, etc.) to set up joint ventures with European suppliers (OVH, Thalès, etc.)

This would have ensured that our data would be adequately protected against US (Cloud Act) and Chinese (Chinese National Intelligence Law) extraterritorial laws, which authorise their governments to copy such data, wherever it is located, on grounds of ‘national security’. However, the specialised press revealed at the beginning of April 2024 that these recommendations had disappeared from ENISA’s latest work plan.
Europe’s major digital players rightly voiced their concern in a letter to the Commission. 1.
Does the Commission support the deletion of these recommendations?
How does it intend to protect the most sensitive data from extraterritorial foreign laws?
answer: The Commission is responsible for ensuring compliance with the Cybersecurity Act (1) (CSA) in the development process of European cybersecurity certification schemes.

The draft candidate European Cybersecurity Certification Scheme for Cloud Services (EUCS) scheme is still in its preparatory stage, under development by the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) and will be further discussed among the Member States’ experts in the European Cybersecurity Certification Group (ECCG).

The Commission is supporting the discussions between Member States as chair and secretariat of the ECCG. Once a formal opinion has been issued by the ECCG, ENISA will transmit the candidate scheme to the Commission, who will then prepare an implementing act, to be adopted in accordance with the examination procedure (2).

The Commission's objective, in accordance with the CSA, is for the future EUCS to be a voluntary, risk-based scheme that brings security, transparency and trust to the European cloud market and allows customers to choose the appropriate level of protection, based on their own risk analysis and cost assessment.

Specifically, the objective of the future voluntary scheme would be to harmonise security requirements and conformity assessment methodologies for processing of both non-personal and personal data by a wide range of cloud services and cloud capabilities that they implement, including application, infrastructure and platform.
This is expected to foster the uptake of cloud technologies and improve the EU’s cybersecurity landscape to ensure that European data is cybersecure regardless of where it is processed.

Regulation (EU) 2019/881 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 April 2019 on ENISA (the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity) and on information and communications technology cybersecurity certification and repealing Regulation (EU) No 526/2013 (Cybersecurity Act). Article 49 (6) and (7) of the Cybersecurity Act.
